# Airbnb
### **System Design: Airbnb**
This document outlines the architecture for a scalable, highly available, and consistent accommodation booking platform. We will break down the system into its core components, explain the technology choices, and walk through key user flows.

### 1. System Overview & Core Principles

The architecture will be based on a **Microservices** pattern. This approach decouples different functional areas of the platform User Management, Search, Bookings) into independent, scalable services. This enhances maintainability, fault isolation, and allows teams to work autonomously.

**Core Principles:**
*   **Database per Service:** Each microservice owns its data and has its own database. This prevents a single database from becoming a bottleneck and allows for choosing the right database technology for the job.
*   **Asynchronous Communication:** Services communicate asynchronously via a message queue (like Apache Kafka) for non-critical operations sending a confirmation email after a booking is made). This improves resilience and responsiveness.
*   **API-First Design:** All functionality is exposed through a versioned, secure, and well-documented RESTful API, consumed by our web and mobile clients.
*   **Cloud-Native:** The entire system is designed to run on a cloud platform AWS, GCP, Azure) to leverage managed services, auto-scaling, and global infrastructure.

### 2. High-Level Architecture Diagram

This diagram illustrates the major components and their interactions.

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph "Clients"
        WebApp[Web Client]
        MobileApp[Mobile App]
    end

    subgraph "Global Infrastructure"
        CDN[CDN CloudFront]
        WAF[Web Application Firewall]
        APIGateway[API Gateway]
        MainLB[Load Balancer]
    end

    subgraph "Core Microservices"
        UserService[User Service - PostgreSQL]
        ListingService[Listing Service - PostgreSQL/PostGIS]
        SearchService[Search Service - Elasticsearch]
        BookingService[Booking Service - PostgreSQL]
        PaymentService[Payment Service - PostgreSQL PCI]
        ReviewService[Review Service - Cassandra/DynamoDB]
        MessagingService[Messaging Service - WebSocket/Cassandra]
        NotificationService[Notification Service]
    end

    subgraph "Data and Infrastructure"
        S3[Object Storage - for Media]
        Redis[Distributed Cache Redis - for Calendars Sessions]
        Kafka[Message Queue - Kafka]
        Monitoring[Monitoring and Alerting - Prometheus/Grafana]
        Logging[Centralized Logging - ELK Stack]
    end

    subgraph "Third-Party Integrations"
        Stripe[Payment Gateway - Stripe/PayPal]
        GoogleMaps[Maps and Geocoding API]
        FCM[Push Notifications - FCM/APNS]
        Twilio[SMS/Email Gateway - Twilio/SES]
    end

    %% Connections
    WebApp --> CDN
    MobileApp --> CDN
    CDN --> WAF
    WAF --> APIGateway
    APIGateway --> MainLB
    MainLB --> UserService
    MainLB --> ListingService
    MainLB --> SearchService
    MainLB --> BookingService
    MainLB --> PaymentService
    MainLB --> ReviewService
    MainLB --> MessagingService

    ListingService -- CRUD Ops --> S3
    ListingService -- Geodata --> GoogleMaps
    ListingService -- Publishes listing_updated --> Kafka

    SearchIngestor[Search Ingestor] -- Consumes --> Kafka
    SearchIngestor -- Indexes Data --> SearchService

    BookingService -- Initiates Payment --> PaymentService
    PaymentService -- Processes via --> Stripe
    Stripe -- Webhook --> PaymentService
    BookingService -- Uses for Locks --> Redis
    BookingService -- Publishes booking_confirmed --> Kafka

    ReviewService -- Publishes new_review --> Kafka
    MessagingService -- Publishes new_message --> Kafka

    NotificationService -- Consumes Events --> Kafka
    NotificationService --> FCM
    NotificationService --> Twilio

    UserService --> APIGateway
    SearchService --> APIGateway
    BookingService --> APIGateway
```

### 3. Deep Dive into Core Services

#### A. User Service
*   **Responsibilities:** Handles user authentication (including OAuth with Google/Facebook), registration, profile management, and password storage.
*   **Technology:**
    *   **Database:** PostgreSQL. A relational database is ideal for storing user data with strong consistency and well-defined schemas.
    *   **Logic:** Stores hashed passwords (using bcrypt), manages user sessions, and handles PII data encryption at rest.

#### B. Listing Service
*   **Responsibilities:** Manages CRUD operations for property listings. This includes descriptions, amenities, pricing rules, and host information.
*   **Technology:**
    *   **Database:** PostgreSQL with the **PostGIS** extension. PostGIS is crucial for efficient geospatial queries "find all listings within a 5-mile radius").
    *   **Media Storage:** All images and videos are uploaded directly to an **Object Storage** service like Amazon S3. The Listing Service only stores the S3 URLs. This offloads heavy file serving and scales independently.
    *   **Integration:** When a listing is created or updated, it publishes an event `listing_updated`) to Kafka.

#### C. Search Service
*   **Responsibilities:** Provides fast, advanced search and filtering capabilities. This is a read-heavy service optimized for low latency.
*   **Technology:**
    *   **Search Engine:** **Elasticsearch**. It is purpose-built for full-text search, complex filtering, geo-searches, and relevance-based ranking.
    *   **Data Ingestion:** A separate "Search Ingestor" service listens to `listing_updated` events from Kafka. It fetches the latest listing data from the Listing Service and indexes it into Elasticsearch. This decouples the write path (Listing Service) from the read path (Search Service), ensuring high performance for both.

#### D. Booking Service
*   **Responsibilities:** Manages the entire booking lifecycle: checking availability, creating reservations, handling cancellations, and maintaining booking status. This is the most critical service for transactional integrity.
*   **Technology:**
    *   **Database:** PostgreSQL. We need **ACID** transactions to prevent double bookings and ensure data integrity.
    *   **Calendar/Availability Cache:** A **Distributed Cache** like **Redis** is used to store availability data for properties. This allows for extremely fast availability checks (<10ms) without hitting the primary database for every search query. When a booking is confirmed, the Redis cache is updated along with the primary database.

#### E. Payment Service
*   **Responsibilities:** Handles all financial transactions. It integrates with third-party payment gateways and ensures security and compliance.
*   **Technology:**
    *   **Database:** PostgreSQL for tracking transaction states.
    *   **Security:** This service must be **PCI DSS compliant**. It operates in a highly isolated environment. It never stores raw credit card numbers; instead, it deals with tokens provided by payment gateways like **Stripe** or **PayPal**.
    *   **Workflow:** It communicates with the Booking Service via events. When a booking is initiated, it creates a payment intent. It receives webhooks from the payment gateway to confirm payment success or failure.

#### F. Review Service
*   **Responsibilities:** Manages the two-sided review system for guests and hosts.
*   **Technology:**
    *   **Database:** A NoSQL database like **Apache Cassandra** or **Amazon DynamoDB**. This is a write-heavy system, and NoSQL databases provide the horizontal scalability and write performance needed. Eventual consistency is acceptable for reviews.

#### G. Messaging Service
*   **Responsibilities:** Facilitates real-time chat between guests and hosts.
*   **Technology:**
    *   **Protocol:** **WebSockets** for persistent, bidirectional communication between clients and the server. The API Gateway can manage WebSocket connections.
    *   **Database:** **Cassandra** or **DynamoDB** is excellent for storing chat history, as it's a time-series data pattern that scales well with high write volumes.

#### H. Notification Service
*   **Responsibilities:** Sends notifications (push, email, SMS) to users based on system events.
*   **Technology:**
    *   **Logic:** This is a stateless service that consumes events from Kafka `booking_confirmed`, `new_message`, `review_reminder`).
    *   **Integrations:** It uses third-party services like **Amazon SES/Twilio** for emails/SMS and **Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM)/Apple Push Notification Service (APNS)** for push notifications.

---

### 4. Detailed Workflow Walkthroughs

#### A. Workflow: Search for a Property (Latency < 200ms)

1.  **Client Request:** The user enters a location, dates, and filters "Pool," "Wi-Fi") on the web or mobile app. The request hits the API Gateway.
2.  **API Gateway:** Routes the request to the **Search Service**.
3.  **Search Service:**
    *   Constructs a complex query for **Elasticsearch**.
    *   The query includes a `bool` query with `must` clauses for filters (amenities), a `geo_distance` query for location, and a `range` query for dates.
    *   It also computes a relevance score based on factors like location, review scores, and host responsiveness.
4.  **Availability Check:** For the top N results from Elasticsearch, the Search Service makes a quick, parallelized call to the **Redis** cache to get real-time availability for the requested dates, filtering out any unavailable listings.
5.  **Response:** The Search Service compiles the final list of available properties and returns it to the client. This entire process is highly optimized to meet the sub-200ms latency requirement.

#### B. Workflow: Book a Property (Strong Consistency)

This flow uses a **Saga Pattern** to manage a distributed transaction across the Booking and Payment services, ensuring data consistency without a single, monolithic database transaction.

1.  **Client Request:** User clicks "Reserve" for a specific property and dates. The request hits the API Gateway, which routes it to the **Booking Service**.
2.  **Lock & Create Pending Booking:**
    *   The **Booking Service** first attempts to acquire a **distributed lock** on the `property_id` and `dates` using **Redis**. This prevents anyone else from booking the same dates simultaneously.
    *   If the lock is acquired, it checks its primary PostgreSQL database for availability one last time (as the source of truth).
    *   It then creates a booking record in its database with the status `PENDING`. The lock is held with a short TTL 15 minutes).
3.  **Initiate Payment:** The Booking Service makes a synchronous API call to the **Payment Service**, requesting it to create a payment intent.
4.  **Process Payment:**
    *   The **Payment Service** communicates with **Stripe**, gets a payment token, and sends it back to the client via the Booking Service.
    *   The client uses this token to submit payment information directly to Stripe.
5.  **Payment Confirmation (Webhook):**
    *   Stripe processes the payment and sends a webhook to a secure endpoint on our **Payment Service** to confirm the transaction was successful.
6.  **Confirm Booking (Saga Choreography):**
    *   Upon receiving the success webhook, the **Payment Service** updates its internal state and publishes a `payment_successful` event to **Kafka**.
    *   The **Booking Service** is subscribed to this topic. When it consumes the `payment_successful` event, it updates the booking status from `PENDING` to `CONFIRMED`.
    *   It then releases the distributed lock in Redis.
    *   Finally, it publishes a `booking_confirmed` event to Kafka.
7.  **Notifications:** The **Notification Service** consumes the `booking_confirmed` event and sends confirmation emails and push notifications to the guest and host.

**Failure Handling:**
*   If the payment fails (Stripe webhook reports failure), the Payment Service publishes a `payment_failed` event. The Booking Service consumes this, changes the booking status to `FAILED`, and releases the lock.
*   If the user abandons the payment, the lock in Redis will expire after its TTL, and a background job in the Booking Service will change the `PENDING` booking to `CANCELLED`.

---

### 5. Addressing Non-Functional Requirements

*   **Scalability:** All services are stateless and can be horizontally scaled independently. The use of Kafka and managed cloud databases (like AWS RDS/Aurora, DynamoDB) allows the data layer to scale as well.
*   **High Availability (99.99%):**
    *   **Multi-Region/Multi-AZ:** The entire infrastructure is deployed across multiple Availability Zones (AZs) within a region. For disaster recovery, a hot-standby deployment is maintained in a secondary region.
    *   **Load Balancing & Health Checks:** Load balancers distribute traffic and automatically route it away from unhealthy service instances.
*   **Latency:** Achieved via CDNs for static assets, globally distributed read replicas for databases, extensive caching (Redis, and using optimized search engines (Elasticsearch).
*   **Consistency:** Strong consistency is enforced within individual services using ACID-compliant databases (PostgreSQL). For distributed transactions across services, the Saga pattern is used to ensure eventual consistency and business-level integrity.
*   **Security:**
    *   **WAF:** Protects against common web exploits (SQL injection, XSS).
    *   **PII Encryption:** All sensitive user data is encrypted at rest and in transit (TLS).
    *   **PCI Compliance:** The Payment Service is isolated and built to strict PCI DSS standards.
    *   **Fraud Detection:** A separate real-time fraud detection service can analyze booking patterns new account, high-value booking, suspicious IP) and flag them for review.
*   **Observability:**
    *   **Logging:** Centralized logging using the ELK Stack (Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana).
    *   **Metrics:** Services export metrics to Prometheus, which are visualized in Grafana dashboards.
    *   **Tracing:** Distributed tracing Jaeger, OpenTelemetry) is implemented to trace requests as they flow through multiple microservices.
    *   **Alerting:** Automated alerts via Alertmanager) are configured for high error rates, latency spikes, or system downtime.

constraints: Stream latency < 500ms
Support 100M+ monthly active users
99.95% uptime

Collaborative playlists: Use CRDTs (Conflict-Free Replicated Data Types)

sample_solution:
# Spotify Playlist
# System Design: Collaborative Music Streaming Service
This document outlines the architecture for a music streaming service with a focus on collaborative playlists, low-latency streaming, and personalized recommendations, designed to scale to over 100 million monthly active users (MAU).

## 1. Core Principles & Architecture Overview

We will use a **microservices architecture**. This approach breaks down the large, complex application into smaller, independent services. This enhances scalability, fault tolerance, and allows teams to develop and deploy their services independently.

The main components are:
*   **API Gateway:** A single entry point for all client requests, handling routing, authentication, and rate limiting.
*   **Client Applications:** Web, desktop, and mobile apps.
*   **Core Services:** Microservices for handling users, metadata, playlists, etc.
*   **Streaming Pipeline:** A dedicated infrastructure for ingesting, processing, and delivering audio content globally.
*   **Data & ML Pipeline:** A backend system for collecting user interaction data, training recommendation models, and processing royalty payments.

### Mermaid Diagram of High-Level Architecture

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph "Client Tier"
        UserApp[Client App - Mobile/Web/Desktop]
    end

    subgraph "API & Core Services"
        API_Gateway[API Gateway]
        UserService[User Service]
        MetadataService[Metadata Service]
        PlaylistService[Playlist Service - CRDTs]
        SearchService[Search Service]
        RecommendationService[Recommendation Service]
    end

    subgraph "Streaming Infrastructure"
        StreamingService[Streaming Service]
        CDN[Global Content Delivery Network - CDN]
        Transcoding[Audio Transcoding Pipeline]
        BlobStore[Raw Audio Storage - S3/GCS]
    end

    subgraph "Data & Analytics Pipeline"
        PlaybackTracker[Playback Tracking Service]
        Kafka[Message Queue - Kafka]
        DataLake[Data Lake - S3]
        Spark[Spark Processing Jobs]
        ML_Training[ML Model Training]
        RoyaltyService[Royalty Calculation Service]
    end

    subgraph "Databases & Caches"
        UserDB[(User DB)]
        MetadataDB[(Metadata DB)]
        PlaylistDB[(Playlist DB)]
        SearchIndex[(Search Index)]
        RecsCache[(Recommendations Cache)]
    end

    %% Connections
    UserApp --> API_Gateway

    API_Gateway --> UserService
    API_Gateway --> MetadataService
    API_Gateway --> PlaylistService
    API_Gateway --> SearchService
    API_Gateway --> RecommendationService
    API_Gateway --> StreamingService

    UserService --> UserDB
    MetadataService --> MetadataDB
    PlaylistService --> PlaylistDB
    SearchService --> SearchIndex
    RecommendationService --> RecsCache

    %% Streaming Flow
    StreamingService --> CDN
    Transcoding --> CDN
    BlobStore --> Transcoding

    %% Data Pipeline Flow
    UserApp -- "Play Event" --> PlaybackTracker
    PlaybackTracker --> Kafka
    Kafka --> DataLake
    Spark --> DataLake
    Spark --> ML_Training
    Spark --> RoyaltyService
    ML_Training --> RecsCache

    %% Real-time Collaboration
    UserApp -- WebSocket --> PlaylistService
```

---

## 2. Step-by-Step Deep Dive into Core Components

### Step 1: Audio Streaming (< 500ms Latency using HLS/DASH)

The goal is fast, reliable, global audio delivery.

1.  **Ingestion:** Record labels upload high-quality, lossless audio files WAV, FLAC) to a secure internal portal. These files are stored in a durable object storage like **Amazon S3** or **Google Cloud Storage**.

2.  **Transcoding & Segmentation:**
    *   An automated pipeline using AWS Lambda or a dedicated server fleet) triggers on every new upload.
    *   This pipeline **transcodes** the source audio into multiple formats and bitrates 96kbps AAC, 160kbps AAC, 320kbps Opus) to support adaptive streaming for users with varying network conditions.
    *   Each transcoded file is then segmented into small chunks 2-6 seconds long) according to the **HLS (HTTP Live Streaming)** or **DASH (Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP)** protocol.
    *   A **manifest file** `.m3u8` for HLS) is created. This manifest is a playlist of the audio chunks and contains information about the available bitrates.

3.  **Distribution:**
    *   All audio chunks and manifest files are pushed to a **Content Delivery Network (CDN)** like CloudFront, Akamai, or Cloudflare.
    *   The CDN caches these files in edge locations around the world, physically close to the users.

4.  **Playback:**
    *   When a user presses play, the client app requests the song's manifest URL from our `Metadata Service`.
    *   The client's built-in media player fetches the manifest from the **nearest CDN edge location**.
    *   The player reads the manifest, determines the best bitrate for the current network condition, and starts downloading the audio chunks sequentially from the CDN.
    *   This process ensures **low latency (< 500ms)** because the data travels a very short distance from the local CDN edge server to the user's device.

### Step 2: Collaborative Playlists (using CRDTs)

This feature allows multiple users to add, remove, and reorder songs in a shared playlist simultaneously without conflicts.

1.  **Why CRDTs?** Traditional systems use locks to prevent conflicts, which is slow and doesn't work well in an offline-first mobile world. **Conflict-Free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs)** are data structures that are mathematically guaranteed to converge to the same state, even when updates are made concurrently without coordination.

2.  **Data Structure Choice:** We'll use a **Sequence CRDT** (like LSEQ or Logoot) to represent the ordered list of songs in a playlist. In simple terms, each song in the playlist is assigned a unique, fractional position identifier.
    *   When a user adds a song between song A and song B, the client generates a new identifier that falls between A's and B's identifiers A is at position `1.0`, B is at `2.0`, the new song gets `1.5`).
    *   Reordering is simply changing the identifier. Deleting is a tombstone/flag.

3.  **The Workflow:**
    *   **Initial Load:** When a user opens a collaborative playlist, they fetch the current state from the `Playlist Service`.
    *   **Local Edit:** User A adds a song. The client app **immediately** updates the local UI for a responsive feel. It generates a CRDT "operation" `insert(song_id, position_id)`).
    *   **Synchronization:**
        *   This operation is sent to the `Playlist Service` via a persistent **WebSocket** connection.
        *   The `Playlist Service` validates the operation, merges it into its master state (stored in a database like Cassandra or DynamoDB), and broadcasts the operation to all other connected collaborators on that playlist via their WebSockets.
    *   **Convergence:** When User B's client receives the operation from the WebSocket, it applies it to its local CRDT replica. Because the operations are commutative and associative, the order of application doesn't matter. Both User A and User B will see the exact same playlist state eventually. This works even if users are temporarily offline and sync their changes later.

### Step 3: Recommendations (ML on User History)

The goal is to provide personalized content like "Discover Weekly" and "Daily Mix."

1.  **Data Collection:**
    *   The client app sends events for every significant user interaction (play, skip, pause, add to playlist, search, like) to the high-throughput `Playback Tracking Service`.
    *   This service is a simple API that validates the event and pushes it into a **Kafka** message queue. Kafka acts as a durable, scalable buffer that decouples the data producers (clients) from the consumers (processing jobs).

2.  **Data Processing (Batch Pipeline):**
    *   The events from Kafka are streamed into a **Data Lake** S3 partitioned by date) for long-term, cost-effective storage.
    *   A daily or weekly **Apache Spark** job runs on this data lake. It aggregates user listening histories, builds user-item interaction matrices, and processes song metadata/audio features.

3.  **Model Training:**
    *   The Spark job trains several ML models:
        *   **Collaborative Filtering:** Using algorithms like Alternating Least Squares (ALS) to find users with similar tastes and recommend songs they listen to.
        *   **Content-Based Filtering:** Using audio features (extracted from the raw audio) and metadata (genre, artist) to recommend songs that are acoustically similar to what a user likes.
        *   **Natural Language Processing (NLP):** Analyzing playlist names and song lyrics to understand context and mood.

4.  **Serving Recommendations:**
    *   The trained models are used to pre-compute recommendations for every active user.
    *   These recommendations a list of `song_id`s) are stored in a low-latency key-value store or cache like **Redis** or **DynamoDB**, indexed by `user_id`.
    *   When the user opens their app, the `Recommendation Service` is called. It simply fetches the pre-computed list for that `user_id` from the cache and returns it, ensuring a fast response.

### Step 4: Licensing and Royalty Calculation

This is a critical business requirement to pay artists and rights holders.

1.  **Leverage the Data Pipeline:** The same playback event data stored in the Data Lake for recommendations is used for royalty calculations. This is highly efficient as we collect the data once and use it for multiple purposes.

2.  **Royalty Calculation Job:**
    *   A separate, typically monthly, batch job (can also be a Spark job) runs on the Data Lake.
    *   It accurately aggregates the total number of plays for every single track within the pay period.
    *   This play count data is joined with a `Metadata DB` that contains complex licensing information who owns the master recording rights, who owns the publishing rights, what percentage each party gets).
    *   The service calculates the total royalty pool (based on subscription revenue and ad revenue) and distributes it to rights holders based on their proportion of total streams.

3.  **Reporting:** The `Royalty Service` generates detailed reports for the finance department and for external rights holders.

## 3. Scalability and High Availability (100M+ MAU, 99.95% Uptime)

*   **Load Balancing:** An API Gateway and Load Balancers are placed in front of all microservices to distribute traffic evenly.
*   **Horizontal Scaling:** All services are stateless and can be scaled horizontally by simply adding more instances.
*   **Database Scaling:**
    *   **Read-heavy services** (Metadata) use read replicas to scale read operations.
    *   **Write-heavy services** (Playback Tracking, Playlists) use sharded/partitioned databases Cassandra, DynamoDB, or a sharded SQL DB like Vitess) to distribute the write load.
*   **Global Distribution:** Services and databases are deployed across multiple geographic regions US-East, EU-West, AP-Southeast) to reduce latency for users worldwide and provide disaster recovery.
*   **Asynchronous Communication:** Using message queues - Kafka for non-critical operations (like tracking) prevents system failure if a downstream service is slow or unavailable.
*   **Redundancy & Failover:** Every component has redundant copies. If one server or database node fails, traffic is automatically rerouted to a healthy one. This is key to achieving 99.95% uptime.

constraints: ETA accuracy within 10%
Handle 10M+ ETA requests per minute

sample_solution:
# Uber ETA
# Uber ETA System Design
## 1. Overview and Core Challenges

The goal is to design a highly scalable, low-latency, and accurate system to provide Estimated Time of Arrival (ETA) for a ride-hailing service. This involves two main calculations:
1.  **ETA to Pickup:** The time it will take for the assigned driver to reach the rider's pickup location.
2.  **ETA to Destination:** The total time for the trip from the pickup point to the final destination.

The primary challenges are:
*   **Massive Scale:** Handling millions of drivers and riders concurrently.
*   **Real-Time Data:** Processing a constant stream of location updates and traffic changes.
*   **Accuracy:** Providing ETAs that riders and drivers can trust, despite unpredictable real-world conditions.

## 2. System Architecture: Core Components

We will use a microservices-based architecture to ensure scalability, resilience, and maintainability.



### Mermaid Diagram Code

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph "Client Applications"
        RiderApp("Rider App")
        DriverApp("Driver App")
    end

    subgraph "Backend Services"
        APIGateway("API Gateway")
        LocationService("Location Service")
        ETAService("ETA Calculation Service")
        TripService("Trip Management Service")
        NotificationService("Notification Service")
        MLService("Machine Learning Service")
        DataIntegrator("3rd Party Data Integrator")
    end

    subgraph "Data and Infrastructure"
        Kafka[Kafka - Event Stream]
        GeoDB[Geospatial DB - PostGIS/Elasticsearch]
        Cache[Cache - Redis]
        DataLake[Data Lake - S3/HDFS]
        APIs[3rd Party APIs - Google Maps, HERE]
    end

    %% Connections
    RiderApp -- 1. Request Ride / ETA --> APIGateway
    DriverApp -- 2. Continuous Location Pings --> APIGateway

    APIGateway --> TripService
    APIGateway -- Location Pings --> LocationService

    TripService -- 3. Find nearby drivers --> LocationService
    LocationService -- 4. Query drivers by location --> GeoDB
    LocationService -- 5. List of nearby drivers --> TripService

    TripService -- 6. Request ETA for each driver --> ETAService
    ETAService -- 7. Get real-time traffic --> DataIntegrator
    ETAService -- 8. Get predictive data --> MLService
    ETAService -- 9. Get driver location --> LocationService
    ETAService -- 10. Calculate ETA --> TripService

    TripService -- 11. Assign driver, notify --> NotificationService
    NotificationService -- Push ETA --> RiderApp
    NotificationService -- Push ETA --> DriverApp

    %% Real-time Update Loop
    LocationService -- Driver location update --> Kafka
    Kafka -- Location Stream --> ETAService
    ETAService -- Recalculate and Push Update --> NotificationService

    %% Data Pipeline
    LocationService -- "Log Data" --> DataLake
    TripService -- "Log Data" --> DataLake
    DataLake -- "Train Models" --> MLService
    DataIntegrator -- "Fetch Traffic/Weather" --> APIs
```

## 3. Detailed Step-by-Step Workflow

We'll break down the process into two key scenarios: the initial ETA calculation when a ride is requested, and the continuous updates during a trip.

### Scenario 1: Initial ETA Request (Rider books a ride)

This workflow calculates the ETA for multiple nearby drivers so the rider can see how far away their potential ride is.

**Step 1: Rider Requests a Ride**
*   The **Rider App** sends a request to the backend via the **API Gateway**. The request includes the rider's ID, pickup coordinates, and destination coordinates.

**Step 2: Find Nearby Drivers**
*   The **API Gateway** routes the request to the **Trip Management Service**.
*   The **Trip Service** needs to find available drivers near the pickup location. It queries the **Location Service**.
*   The **Location Service** performs a geospatial query on its database PostgreSQL with PostGIS) to find all available drivers within a certain radius 5km). This is highly optimized using a geospatial index like an R-tree.

**Step 3: Calculate ETA for Each Driver**
*   For each nearby driver found, the **Trip Service** asks the **ETA Calculation Service** for two ETAs:
    1.  Driver's current location to the pickup point.
    2.  Pickup point to the final destination.
*   This step is crucial for matching the rider with the most suitable driver.

**Step 4: The ETA Calculation Engine in Action**
*   The **ETA Service** receives a request with `(start_coords, end_coords, vehicle_type, timestamp)`.
*   **a. Routing:** It first determines the most likely route using a routing algorithm like A* on a pre-loaded road network graph from OpenStreetMap). This graph divides the map into road segments (edges) and intersections (nodes).
*   **b. Data Enrichment:** For each segment in the route, it gathers data from multiple sources:
    *   **Real-Time Traffic:** It queries the **3rd Party Data Integrator** (which calls Google Maps/HERE APIs) for current traffic conditions congestion, accidents).
    *   **Predictive Model:** It queries the **ML Service** for a predicted travel time for that segment based on the time of day, day of the week, and vehicle type. This model is trained on historical trip data.
    *   **Static Data:** It uses the segment's length and speed limit as a baseline.
*   **c. Final Calculation:** The service combines these data points using a weighted formula to get the most accurate travel time for each segment. Summing these up gives the final ETA.
    *   `Final_ETA = Σ (Segment_Time)`
    *   `Segment_Time = f(base_time, real_time_traffic_multiplier, historical_prediction)`

**Step 5: Display ETA to Rider**
*   The **ETA Service** returns the calculated ETAs to the **Trip Service**.
*   The **Trip Service** dispatches the request to the best-suited driver and sends the final pickup ETA to the rider via the **Notification Service** (using WebSockets or push notifications).

### Scenario 2: In-Trip Real-Time ETA Updates

Once a trip starts, the ETA must be continuously updated to reflect the driver's progress and changing traffic conditions.

**Step 1: Continuous Location Pings**
*   The **Driver App** continuously sends location data (latitude, longitude, speed, bearing) to the backend every few seconds.
*   **Edge Computing:** To reduce noise and server load, the driver's phone first applies a **Kalman Filter** to the raw GPS data. This algorithm smooths out inaccuracies and provides a more precise location estimate before sending it to the server.

**Step 2: Ingesting and Processing Location Data**
*   The location pings hit the **API Gateway** and are forwarded to the **Location Service**.
*   The **Location Service** updates the driver's current position in the **Geospatial DB**.
*   Simultaneously, it publishes a `driverLocationUpdated` event to a **Kafka** topic. This decouples the location update from the ETA recalculation.

**Step 3: Triggering a Recalculation**
*   The **ETA Service** is a consumer of the `driverLocationUpdated` Kafka topic.
*   When it receives an event for a driver on an active trip, it checks if a recalculation is necessary if the driver has deviated from the original route or if a certain amount of time has passed).

**Step 4: Recalculating the ETA**
*   The **ETA Service** repeats the calculation process from **Scenario 1, Step 4**, but this time using the driver's *new* current location as the starting point for the remainder of the trip to the destination.

**Step 5: Pushing Updates to Clients**
*   The newly calculated ETA is sent to the **Notification Service**.
*   The **Notification Service** pushes the update in real-time to both the **Rider App** and the **Driver App**, ensuring both parties have the latest information.

## 4. Addressing Non-Functional Requirements

**1. High Scalability (100,000+ QPS):**
*   **Horizontal Scaling:** All services (API Gateway, Location, ETA) are stateless and can be scaled horizontally behind a load balancer.
*   **Message Queues - Kafka:** Decouples services. The high-volume firehose of location pings is handled by Kafka, preventing the ETA service from being overwhelmed.
*   **Database Sharding:** The Geospatial DB can be sharded by geographic region S2 cell IDs) to distribute the load.

**2. Low Latency (sub-100ms P99):**
*   **Caching:** Use Redis to cache common ETA requests airport to downtown during rush hour) and pre-computed route graphs.
*   **In-Memory Computation:** The road network graph is loaded into the memory of the ETA service for fast A* traversal.
*   **Edge Computing:** The Kalman filter on the device reduces the amount of noisy data sent to the backend, simplifying server-side processing.
*   **Optimized Geospatial Queries:** Using efficient indexes (R-tree/Quadtree) in PostGIS/Elasticsearch ensures that finding nearby drivers is extremely fast.

**3. High Availability (99.99%):**
*   **Redundancy:** Deploy services across multiple availability zones (AZs) and regions.
*   **Failover:** Use load balancers with health checks to automatically route traffic away from unhealthy instances.
*   **Graceful Degradation:** This is critical.
    *   If the **3rd Party Traffic API** is down, the ETA service falls back to using only the **ML Service's** historical predictions.
    *   If the **ML Service** is down, it falls back to using only real-time traffic data.
    *   If both are down, it falls back to a simple calculation based on distance and speed limits from the road graph. The ETA will be less accurate, but the service remains available.

**4. High Accuracy (within ±1-2 minutes):**
*   **Hybrid Model:** The core of our accuracy comes from combining real-time data, predictive ML models, and static data. This fusion provides a more robust estimate than any single source.
*   **Continuous Learning:** The ML models are continuously retrained on new trip data from the **Data Lake**, allowing the system to adapt to new traffic patterns, road constructions, and city growth.
*   **Vehicle-Specific Profiles:** The ETA model incorporates profiles for different vehicle types UberX vs. UberXL), which may have different acceleration and average speeds.

**5. Extensibility:**
*   **Microservices:** The architecture makes it easy to add new services or modify existing ones without impacting the entire system.
*   **Configurable Models:** Adding a new vehicle type is a matter of adding a new speed profile configuration. Expanding to a new city involves loading a new road network graph and training a region-specific ML model.
*   **Data Integrator:** This service acts as an abstraction layer, making it simple to add new data sources weather APIs, public event calendars) to further improve ETA accuracy.

Provide total trip ETA from pickup to destination, updated dynamically as the driver progresses.
Integrate real-time traffic data (congestion, accidents, road closures) to adjust ETA calculations.
Continuously update driver locations and recalculate ETAs based on their movement.
Utilize historical trip data and machine learning models for predictive ETA accuracy.
Support different vehicle types (e.g., UberX, UberXL) with varying speed profiles.
Adjust ETAs based on surge pricing and special events affecting traffic.
Provide ETA updates to rider and driver applications in real-time.

Achieve sub-100ms P99 latency for ETA calculations.
Maintain 99.99% availability for the ETA service.
Ensure high accuracy for ETA predictions, ideally within ±1-2 minutes under normal conditions.
Implement graceful degradation for ETA calculations if real-time traffic data or ML models are temporarily unavailable.

# Amazon Shopping Cart
### **Amazon Shopping Cart: System Design**
This document outlines the design for a shopping cart system that meets the functional and non-functional requirements of a large-scale e-commerce platform like Amazon.

### **1. Core Design Principles & Strategy**

To meet the demanding requirements of high availability, low latency, and global scale, our design will be based on the following principles:

*   **Multi-Region Active-Active Deployment:** To ensure high availability and low latency for a global user base, the service will be deployed in multiple geographic regions. Users will be routed to the nearest region.
*   **Stateless Service Layer:** The application servers (Shopping Cart Service) will be stateless. All user cart data will be stored in a centralized, distributed database and cache, allowing any server to handle any user's request.
*   **Decoupled Architecture:** The Shopping Cart Service will be an independent microservice, communicating with other services (Product, Checkout) via well-defined APIs. This prevents cascading failures.
*   **Data-Driven Decisions:** The choice of database and caching technology is critical. We need a solution that supports multi-region writes, horizontal scaling, and low-latency operations.
*   **Asynchronous Operations for Non-Critical Paths:** While core cart operations (add, view) must be fast, related tasks can be handled asynchronously to improve responsiveness.

### **2. High-Level Architecture**

The system is composed of several key components working together across multiple regions.

  *(A conceptual visualization of the Mermaid diagram below)*

#### **Mermaid Diagram Code**

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph User
        direction LR
        U(Browser/Mobile App)
    end

    subgraph "Global Infrastructure"
        DNS(Route 53 / Global DNS)
        GLB(Global Load Balancer)
    end

    U -- HTTPS Request --> DNS
    DNS -- Latency-based Routing --> GLB

    subgraph "AWS Region: us-east-1 Active"
        direction TB
        RLB1[Regional Load Balancer]
        subgraph "Auto-Scaling Group"
            S1[Cart Service 1]
            S2[Cart Service 2]
            S3[Cart Service N]
        end
        RC1[ElastiCache for Redis]
        DB1[DynamoDB]

        GLB --> RLB1
        RLB1 --> S1
        RLB1 --> S2
        RLB1 --> S3
        S1 --- RC1
        S2 --- RC1
        S3 --- RC1
        S1 --- DB1
        S2 --- DB1
        S3 --- DB1
```

### **3. Step-by-Step Component Breakdown**

#### **Step 1: User Request & Global Routing**
1.  **User Action:** A user clicks "Add to Cart" on their browser or mobile app.
2.  **DNS Resolution:** The request goes to a global DNS service like **Amazon Route 53**.
3.  **Latency-Based Routing:** Route 53 is configured with latency-based routing. It resolves the domain to the IP address of the **Global Load Balancer (GLB)** in the AWS region closest to the user a user in Europe is routed to `eu-west-1`). This minimizes network latency.
4.  **Regional Routing:** The GLB forwards the request to a **Regional Load Balancer (RLB)** within the selected region. The RLB distributes the traffic across a fleet of **Shopping Cart Service** instances.

#### **Step 2: Shopping Cart Service (The Application Logic)**
This is a stateless microservice running on EC2 instances or containers (ECS/EKS) within an Auto-Scaling Group.
1.  **Authentication:** The service first authenticates the user via an auth token JWT) passed in the request header. It extracts the `userId`.
2.  **Request Processing:** The service processes the request Add, Update, View).
3.  **Data Interaction:** It interacts with the caching and database layers to perform the required operations.
4.  **Service Integration:** For operations like viewing a cart, it calls the **Product Service** to fetch real-time price and availability information. When the user proceeds to checkout, it hands off the cart data to the **Checkout Service**.

#### **Step 3: Data Storage & Caching Strategy (The Core of the System)**

This is the most critical part of the design for meeting performance, durability, and availability goals.

1.  **Primary Database: Amazon DynamoDB with Global Tables**
    *   **Why DynamoDB?** It's a fully managed NoSQL database offering single-digit millisecond latency, seamless scalability, and high durability.
    *   **Why Global Tables?** This feature is the key to our active-active multi-region architecture. When data is written to the DynamoDB table in one region `us-east-1`), DynamoDB automatically replicates that write to the tables in other regions (`eu-west-1`). This ensures:
        *   **Low-Latency Writes:** Users write to their local region's database.
        *   **High Availability & Durability:** If a whole region fails, the data is safe in other regions, and traffic can be failed over automatically.
        *   **Zero Data Loss:** Writes are durably stored across multiple facilities and replicated across regions.

2.  **Data Model for DynamoDB:**
    We use a simple key-value/document model.

    *   **Table Name:** `UserCarts`
    *   **Primary Key:**
        *   **Partition Key:** `userId` (ensures all items for a user are stored together for efficient queries).
        *   **Sort Key:** `productId` (allows efficiently targeting a specific item within a cart).
    *   **Attributes:**
        *   `userId`: (String) e.g., "user-12345"
        *   `productId`: (String) e.g., "B08N5HR2DR"
        *   `quantity`: (Number)
        *   `addedTimestamp`: (Number) Unix timestamp
        *   `lastModified`: (Number) Unix timestamp
        *   `ttl`: (Number) Unix timestamp for 30 days in the future, used by DynamoDB to automatically delete expired carts.

3.  **Caching Layer: Amazon ElastiCache for Redis**
    *   **Purpose:** To provide sub-millisecond latency for cart reads (View Cart), which are typically more frequent than writes. This helps us meet the P95 < 50ms requirement for reads.
    *   **Strategy: Write-Through Cache**
        *   **Read Operation (View Cart):**
            1. The Cart Service first attempts to fetch the cart from Redis using the `userId` as the key.
            2. **Cache Hit:** If found, the data is returned immediately. This is the fast path.
            3. **Cache Miss:** If not found, the service queries DynamoDB, populates the Redis cache with the result, sets a Time-To-Live (TTL) on the cache entry 1-2 hours), and then returns the data.
        *   **Write Operation (Add/Update/Remove Item):**
            1. The Cart Service writes the change directly to the **DynamoDB** table. This ensures durability.
            2. After the database write is confirmed, the service **invalidates** the corresponding `userId` key in the Redis cache. Invalidating is often safer and simpler than trying to update the cache, preventing stale data. The next read will be a cache miss, which will then repopulate the cache with fresh data from DynamoDB.

#### **Step 4: Integration with Other Services**

1.  **Product Service:**
    *   **Function:** Provides real-time product data like price, name, image, and availability.
    *   **Interaction:** When a user views their cart, the Cart Service fetches the list of `productId`s and `quantity`s from its own database. It then makes a batch API call to the Product Service to "decorate" this data with the latest details.
    *   **Resilience:** The Cart Service should implement a **Circuit Breaker** pattern when calling the Product Service. If the Product Service is down, the Cart Service can perform **graceful degradation**: it can still display the cart items using cached or last-known data, perhaps with a message like "Live pricing is currently unavailable."

2.  **Checkout Service & Inventory Management**
    *   **The Challenge:** We cannot reserve inventory when an item is added to the cart, as this would lock up stock for millions of users who may never check out. Inventory is only reserved at the final stage of checkout.
    *   **Solution: Compensating Transactions (Saga Pattern)**
        1.  **Initiate Checkout:** The user clicks "Proceed to Checkout." The Cart Service calls the Checkout Service, passing the `userId` and cart contents.
        2.  **Checkout Service Orchestrates:** The Checkout Service starts a "Saga," a sequence of transactions.
        3.  **Inventory Reservation:** It calls the Inventory Service to attempt to reserve the items.
        4.  **Payment Processing:** If inventory is available, it calls the Payment Service.
        5.  **Order Creation:** If payment is successful, it calls the Order Service to create a permanent order.
        6.  **Clear Cart:** Finally, it calls the Cart Service to clear the user's cart.
        7.  **Failure Handling (Compensation):** If the inventory reservation fails item went out of stock), the Saga is rolled back. The Checkout Service executes compensating actions, such as notifying the user and leaving the items in their cart for a future attempt. This ensures consistency without locking resources prematurely.

### **4. Addressing Specific Constraints**

*   **A/B Testing:** This is primarily handled at the edge or on the client-side. A feature flagging service (or CDN logic) can serve different UI versions to different user segments. The backend APIs designed here will support any UI variation, as the core functions (add, view, update) remain the same.
*   **Distributed Sessions:** Our design is inherently stateless, which is superior to sticky sessions. The `userId` is derived from a token (like a JWT) sent with every request. This means any server can handle the request without needing any prior session context, making scaling and failover seamless.
*   **Price Consistency:** Prices are fetched in real-time from the Product Service when the cart is viewed. To reduce load, the Cart Service can cache the *price data* it receives from the Product Service in a separate Redis cache with a very short TTL 1-5 minutes). This balances consistency with performance.
*   **Cart Expiration:** By setting a `ttl` attribute on each cart item in DynamoDB, we can leverage DynamoDB's built-in TTL feature to automatically delete items after 30 days of inactivity, keeping the database clean without any manual cleanup jobs.

# Google Calendar
Here is a detailed, step-by-step solution for designing a scalable Google Calendar system, presented in an easy-to-follow markdown format.
***
# System Design: A Scalable Collaborative Calendar

This document outlines the design for a highly available, scalable, and real-time collaborative calendar system, similar to Google Calendar. We will break down the architecture, data models, and workflows to meet the specified functional and non-functional requirements.

## 1. High-Level Architecture

The system is designed using a microservices architecture to ensure scalability, resilience, and maintainability. Each service has a distinct responsibility and communicates with others through APIs and a message bus - Kafka.

**Core Components:**

1.  **Clients:** Web browsers, mobile applications (iOS, Android) that interact with the system.
2.  **API Gateway:** A single entry point for all client requests. It handles authentication, rate limiting, and routing requests to the appropriate microservice.
3.  **Load Balancer:** Distributes incoming traffic across multiple instances of the API Gateway and backend services to ensure high availability.
4.  **Microservices:**
    *   **Calendar Service:** Manages calendar metadata, including creation, deletion, and sharing permissions.
    *   **Event Service:** The core service responsible for all CRUD operations on events, including handling the complex logic of recurring events and exceptions.
    *   **Sync Service:** Manages real-time updates to clients using WebSockets. It pushes changes to connected users when an event they have access to is modified.
    *   **Notification Service:** Responsible for sending event reminders via email, SMS, or push notifications.
    *   **Search Service:** Provides powerful search and filtering capabilities by indexing event data.
5.  **Data Stores:**
    *   **Event Database (NoSQL - Bigtable/Cassandra):** The primary database for storing event and calendar data. A NoSQL database is chosen for its horizontal scalability and ability to handle massive write loads (1B+ events/day).
    *   **Search Index (Elasticsearch):** A dedicated search engine for fast and complex queries on event data.
    *   **Cache (Redis:** Used for caching frequently accessed data, such as user free/busy schedules and hot event data, to reduce latency.
6.  **Message Bus - Kafka:** An asynchronous backbone for communication between services. It decouples services, making the system more resilient and scalable. For example, when an event is created, the Event Service publishes a message to Kafka, which is then consumed by the Sync, Notification, and Search services.

## 2. Data Schema Design

Efficiently storing recurring events is the biggest challenge. We will not materialize (pre-calculate and store) every instance of a recurring event, as this would lead to a massive storage footprint and difficult updates. Instead, we store the recurrence *rule* and expand it on the fly during read operations.

All timestamps are stored in **UTC**.

#### Table: `Calendars`
Stores metadata for each calendar.
- `calendar_id` (UUID, Partition Key)
- `owner_user_id` (UUID)
- `title` (String)
- `description` (String)
- `timezone` (String)
- `created_at` (Timestamp)
- `updated_at` (Timestamp)

#### Table: `Calendar_Sharing`
Manages permissions for shared calendars.
- `calendar_id` (UUID, Partition Key)
- `shared_with_user_id` (UUID, Clustering Key)
- `permission_level` (Enum: `OWNER`, `EDIT`, `VIEW`)
- `created_at` (Timestamp)

#### Table: `Events`
Stores all event data. This table handles both single-instance and recurring events.
- `event_id` (UUID, Partition Key)
- `calendar_id` (UUID)
- `title` (String)
- `description` (String)
- `location` (String)
- `start_time_utc` (Timestamp)
- `end_time_utc` (Timestamp)
- `timezone` (String, e.g., 'America/New_York')
- `attendees` (JSON/Map: `{'user_id': 'RSVP_STATUS'}`)
- `is_recurring` (Boolean)
- `parent_event_id` (UUID, Nullable) - *If this is an exception, this links to the original recurring event.*
- `rrule` (String, Nullable) - *Stores the recurrence rule, e.g., `FREQ=WEEKLY;BYDAY=MO,WE;UNTIL=20241231T000000Z`. We use the standard iCalendar (RFC 5545) RRULE format.*
- `version` (Integer) - *For conflict resolution.*
- `created_at` (Timestamp)
- `updated_at` (Timestamp)

**Note on `parent_event_id`:**
- For a **single event**, `is_recurring` is `false`, and `rrule` and `parent_event_id` are `null`.
- For a **recurring event master**, `is_recurring` is `true`, `rrule` is set, and `parent_event_id` is `null`.
- For an **exception** (a modified or deleted instance of a recurring event), `is_recurring` is `false`, `rrule` is `null`, and `parent_event_id` points to the master recurring event's `event_id`. Its `start_time_utc` represents the original start time of the instance that is being modified.

## 3. Detailed Workflow Walkthroughs

### Step-by-Step: Creating a New Event

1.  **Client Request:** A user creates a new event in their mobile app. The client sends a `POST /events` request to the API Gateway with event details (title, time, attendees, recurrence rule if any).
2.  **API Gateway:** The gateway authenticates the user's token and routes the request to the **Event Service**.
3.  **Event Service Logic:**
    a. The service validates the input data.
    b. It generates a unique `event_id`.
    c. All timestamps are converted and normalized to UTC.
    d. The event data is written to the **Event DB (Bigtable)**.
4.  **Asynchronous Fan-out:** After a successful database write, the Event Service publishes an `event_created` message to a **Kafka** topic. The message contains the full event data.
5.  **Downstream Consumers:**
    a. **Search Service:** Consumes the message and updates the **Elasticsearch** index to make the new event searchable.
    b. **Sync Service:** Consumes the message, identifies all attendees and users with whom the calendar is shared, and pushes a real-time update via WebSockets to their connected clients.
    c. **Notification Service:** Consumes the message, calculates the reminder time(s), and schedules the reminders. (More on this below).
6.  **Client Response:** The Event Service returns a `201 Created` response with the new `event_id` to the client. The client UI updates instantly.

### Step-by-Step: Viewing a Calendar for a Specific Month

This workflow demonstrates how recurring events are handled efficiently.

1.  **Client Request:** A user navigates to view their calendar for December 2024. The client sends a `GET /calendar/{id}/events?start_date=2024-12-01&end_date=2024-12-31` request.
2.  **API Gateway:** Authenticates and routes the request to the **Event Service**.
3.  **Event Service Logic (The Core of Recurring Events):**
    a. **Query for Single Events:** The service first queries the **Event DB** for all non-recurring events within the requested date range (`start_date` to `end_date`).
    b. **Query for Recurring Rules:** The service queries the **Event DB** for all recurring event *masters* (`is_recurring = true`) whose rules could potentially generate instances within the date range. This query is broad fetch all recurring events that started before the `end_date` and haven't ended before the `start_date`).
    c. **Query for Exceptions:** The service queries the **Event DB** for all exceptions (`parent_event_id` is not null) that fall within the date range.
    d. **On-the-Fly Expansion:** The Event Service now processes the recurring rules in memory. For each rule, it generates the instances that fall within the December 2024 window.
    e. **Apply Exceptions:** It then iterates through the fetched exceptions. If an exception corresponds to a generated instance, it either modifies that instance with the exception's data or removes it (if it was a deletion).
    f. **Merge and Sort:** The service merges the list of single events with the final list of generated recurring instances. The combined list is sorted by start time.
4.  **Response:** The final, materialized list of event instances for December 2024 is sent back to the client.

### Step-by-Step: Sending a Reminder

1.  **Scheduling:** When an event is created or updated, the **Event Service** calculates the absolute UTC timestamp for each reminder. It then publishes a message to a specific Kafka topic, e.g., `reminders_to_schedule`, containing `event_id`, `user_id`, `reminder_time_utc`, and `channel` (email/SMS).
2.  **Notification Service:**
    a. This service consumes messages from the `reminders_to_schedule` topic.
    b. It stores these reminders in a time-series or relational database optimized for time-based queries PostgreSQL or a dedicated scheduler DB).
3.  **Triggering:** A poller within the Notification Service runs every minute (or uses a more advanced scheduler). It queries its database for all reminders due in the current minute (`WHERE reminder_time_utc <= NOW()`).
4.  **Dispatching:** For each due reminder, the service fetches the latest event details from the **Event Service** (to ensure the reminder is still valid and has the latest info). It then dispatches the notification through the appropriate channel calls an email service like SendGrid, an SMS gateway like Twilio, or a push notification service like Firebase).
5.  **Cleanup:** Once sent, the reminder is marked as processed or deleted from the scheduler database.

## 4. Addressing Key Non-Functional Requirements

#### Scalability & Availability (99.99%)
- **Horizontal Scaling:** All microservices are stateless and can be scaled horizontally by adding more instances behind the load balancer.
- **Database Scalability:** Using a distributed NoSQL database like Bigtable or Cassandra allows for linear scaling by adding more nodes to the cluster. Data is partitioned across the cluster by `calendar_id` or a composite key) to distribute the load.
- **Global Distribution:** The system can be deployed across multiple geographic regions. A Global Load Balancer directs users to the nearest region. Data is replicated across regions for low latency reads and disaster recovery.
- **Resiliency:** The use of Kafka for asynchronous communication means that if a downstream service (like Search) is temporarily unavailable, messages will queue up and be processed when it comes back online, preventing data loss.

#### Conflict Resolution
Concurrent edits on a shared event are handled using **Optimistic Locking**.
1.  The `Events` table has a `version` column (an integer or timestamp).
2.  When a client fetches an event to edit, it also receives the current `version` number.
3.  When the client sends an update request (`PUT /events/{id}`), it includes the `version` number it has.
4.  The **Event Service** checks if the `version` number in the request matches the `version` number in the database.
    -   **If they match:** The update is valid. The service processes the change, increments the `version` number in the database, and saves the event.
    -   **If they don't match:** Another user has updated the event in the meantime. The service rejects the update with a `409 Conflict` error. The client is then responsible for re-fetching the latest version of the event and prompting the user to merge their changes.

#### Offline Access
- **Client-Side Database:** The client application (web or mobile) uses a local database IndexedDB for web, SQLite for mobile) to store a local copy of the user's calendars and events.
- **Sync Logic:**
    - When online, the client maintains a WebSocket connection with the **Sync Service** to receive real-time updates.
    - When the user goes offline, the app operates on the local database. All changes (creations, updates, deletions) are logged in a local "outbox" queue.
    - When connectivity is restored, the client's sync engine sends the queued changes to the server one by one. The conflict resolution mechanism (versioning) is crucial here to handle cases where the event was modified on another device while the user was offline.

# Twitter Direct Messages
# System Design: Twitter Direct Messages
This document outlines the architecture for a scalable, real-time Direct Messaging (DM) system similar to Twitter's. We will address all functional and non-functional requirements in a step-by-step manner.

## 1. Core Principles & High-Level Overview

The system is designed around a microservices architecture to ensure scalability, fault tolerance, and maintainability. The core idea is to separate the real-time communication path (for new messages, typing indicators) from the standard request/response path (for sending messages, fetching history).

*   **Real-time Path:** Handled by persistent **WebSocket** connections. This allows the server to push data to clients instantly, which is ideal for new messages, typing indicators, and read receipts.
*   **Standard Path:** Handled by a stateless **REST API** over HTTP. This is used for actions initiated by the user, like sending a message or fetching their chat history.
*   **Data Storage:** A distributed, highly available NoSQL database is chosen for message data due to the massive write load and scale requirements.
*   **Asynchronicity:** A message queue is used to handle offline delivery and decouple services.

## 2. System Components

| Component | Technology | Purpose |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **API Gateway** | NGINX, Kong | Single entry point for all HTTP requests. Handles SSL termination, rate limiting, and routing to backend services. |
| **WebSocket Gateway** | Ktor, Netty, Go | Manages persistent WebSocket connections with millions of clients. Handles real-time event pushing. |
| **Messaging Service** | Go / Java / Scala | The core microservice handling all business logic: sending/receiving messages, managing conversations, and orchestrating other services. |
| **Presence Service** | Go / Elixir | Tracks the online/offline status of users. It maintains a mapping of `user_id` to their connected WebSocket Gateway. |
| **Notification Service** | Go / Python | Manages sending push notifications to mobile devices via APNS (Apple) and FCM (Google). |
| **Media Service** | Python / Node.js | Handles uploading, processing, and storing media files (images, videos). |
| **Message Database** | **Apache Cassandra** | The primary database for storing all message and conversation data. Chosen for its linear scalability, high write throughput, and fault tolerance. |
| **Cache** | **Redis** | Used for storing user session data, presence information (online/offline status), and read receipt states. *Note: Redis is chosen over the suggested Memcached due to its richer data structures and persistence options, making it more versatile for this use case.* |
| **Message Queue** | **RabbitMQ / Kafka** | Decouples services and reliably handles asynchronous tasks like delivering messages to offline users and dispatching push notifications. |
| **Object Storage** | **Amazon S3** | Durable, scalable storage for all media files (images, videos, etc.). |
| **Search Cluster** | **Elasticsearch** | Provides powerful full-text search capabilities over message history. |

## 3. Data Models (Cassandra Schema)

Choosing the right data model is critical for performance in Cassandra. The design is optimized for the most common query patterns.

#### Table 1: `messages`
Stores all messages. The primary key is designed for efficient retrieval of messages within a conversation, sorted chronologically.

```sql
CREATE TABLE messages (
    conversation_id uuid,
    message_id timeuuid, -- A time-based UUID, naturally sorted by time
    sender_id uuid,
    content text,
    media_url text,
    created_at timestamp,
    PRIMARY KEY (conversation_id, message_id)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (message_id DESC);
```
*   **Partition Key:** `conversation_id`. All messages for a single chat are co-located on the same node, making reads very fast.
*   **Clustering Key:** `message_id` (a `timeuuid`). This automatically sorts messages in reverse chronological order within a partition.

#### Table 2: `conversations_by_user`
This table acts as an index to allow a user to quickly retrieve all their conversations, sorted by the most recent activity.

```sql
CREATE TABLE conversations_by_user (
    user_id uuid,
    last_message_timestamp timestamp,
    conversation_id uuid,
    conversation_name text,
    last_message_preview text,
    unread_count int,
    PRIMARY KEY (user_id, last_message_timestamp)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (last_message_timestamp DESC);
```
*   **Partition Key:** `user_id`. All conversations for a user are on one node.
*   **Clustering Key:** `last_message_timestamp`. This ensures a user's inbox is always sorted with the most recent conversation at the top.

#### Table 3: `participants_by_conversation`
Stores the list of users in each conversation. This is crucial for fanning out messages in group chats.

```sql
CREATE TABLE participants_by_conversation (
    conversation_id uuid,
    user_id uuid,
    joined_at timestamp,
    last_seen_message_id timeuuid, -- For read receipts
    PRIMARY KEY (conversation_id, user_id)
);
```
*   **Partition Key:** `conversation_id`. Allows for quick lookup of all participants in a chat.

## 4. Detailed Step-by-Step Workflows

### Flow 1: Sending a Message

Let's trace the journey of a message from Sender A to Recipient B.

**Step 1: Client Sends Message**
*   Sender A's client (mobile/web) makes an `HTTP POST` request to `/v1/messages` with the `conversation_id`, `text`, and any `media` to the **API Gateway**.

**Step 2: Service-Level Processing**
*   The **API Gateway** authenticates the request and routes it to an instance of the **Messaging Service**.
*   The **Messaging Service** generates a unique, time-ordered `message_id` a `timeuuid` or `ULID`).

**Step 3: Storing the Message (Durability)**
*   The **Messaging Service** writes the message to the `messages` table in **Cassandra**.
*   It then updates the `conversations_by_user` table for both Sender A and Recipient B with the new `last_message_timestamp` and `last_message_preview`. This write is idempotent.
*   The service sends an `ACK` (acknowledgment) back to Sender A's client immediately after the database write succeeds. This confirms the message is durably stored.

**Step 4: Real-time Delivery (Fan-out)**
*   The **Messaging Service** queries the `participants_by_conversation` table to get all recipients (in this case, just Recipient B).
*   For each recipient, it checks their online status with the **Presence Service** (which uses the **Redis** cache).

**Step 5a: Online Recipient**
*   If Recipient B is online, the **Presence Service** returns the address of the **WebSocket Gateway** that B is connected to.
*   The **Messaging Service** publishes the new message to a specific topic using a message broker like Redis Pub/Sub or RabbitMQ) that the corresponding **WebSocket Gateway** is subscribed to.
*   The **WebSocket Gateway** receives the message and pushes it down the persistent connection to Recipient B's client. The message is delivered in under 100ms.

**Step 5b: Offline Recipient**
*   If Recipient B is offline, the **Messaging Service** publishes a message job to a **RabbitMQ** queue.
*   The **Notification Service**, a consumer of this queue, picks up the job.
*   It retrieves B's device tokens and sends a push notification via APNS/FCM, alerting them of a new message.
*   When B next opens the app, their client will sync and fetch the new messages from the server using the REST API.

### Flow 2: Typing Indicators

This flow must be extremely low-latency and lightweight.

**Step 1:** As Sender A starts typing, their client sends a `start_typing` event over its active **WebSocket** connection. The event includes the `conversation_id`.

**Step 2:** The **WebSocket Gateway** receives this event and forwards it to the **Messaging Service**.

**Step 3:** The **Messaging Service** fetches the other participants in the conversation from the `participants_by_conversation` table (or a cache).

**Step 4:** It then pushes a `user_A_is_typing` event to the other participants (Recipient B) via their respective **WebSocket Gateways**.

**Step 5:** Recipient B's client receives the event and displays the "A is typing..." indicator.

**Step 6:** If Sender A stops typing for a few seconds or sends the message, the client sends a `stop_typing` event, which follows the same path to remove the indicator.

### Flow 3: Read Receipts

**Step 1:** When Recipient B's client renders a message with `message_id_123` on screen, it sends an `HTTP POST` request to `/v1/conversations/{id}/read` with the `last_seen_message_id`.

**Step 2:** The **API Gateway** routes this to the **Messaging Service**.

**Step 3:** The **Messaging Service** updates the `participants_by_conversation` table in **Cassandra**, setting the `last_seen_message_id` for Recipient B to `message_id_123`.

**Step 4:** To notify the sender in real-time, the **Messaging Service** pushes a `receipt_updated` event (containing the `conversation_id`, `user_id`, and `last_seen_message_id`) to Sender A through their **WebSocket Gateway**.

**Step 5:** Sender A's client receives this event and updates the UI to show a "Read" or "Seen" status on the relevant messages.

## 5. Addressing Non-Functional Requirements

*   **Scalability (10M concurrent users, 1B messages/day):**
    *   All services (API Gateway, WebSocket Gateway, Microservices) are stateless and can be scaled horizontally behind load balancers.
    *   Cassandra and Redis are designed for linear horizontal scaling by adding more nodes to the cluster.
    *   RabbitMQ/Kafka can be clustered to handle the high message throughput.
*   **Low Latency (<100ms):**
    *   WebSockets provide a persistent, low-latency channel for real-time events.
    *   Geo-distributing WebSocket Gateways and Redis caches closer to users (at the edge) can further reduce latency.
    *   Cassandra provides single-digit millisecond read/write performance at scale.
*   **High Availability (99.99%):**
    *   No single point of failure. Every component is redundant and load-balanced across multiple servers and availability zones.
    *   Cassandra's multi-datacenter replication provides exceptional fault tolerance. If one region goes down, the system remains operational.
*   **Strong Consistency & Durability:**
    *   **Durability:** Messages are immediately persisted to Cassandra with a replication factor of 3 (or more). Writes are only acknowledged after being written to a commit log on multiple replicas, preventing data loss.
    *   **Consistency:** For critical operations like message sends, we can use a `QUORUM` consistency level in Cassandra. This ensures that a majority of replicas must acknowledge the write before it's considered successful, guaranteeing strong consistency.
*   **Security:**
    *   **TLS:** All communication between clients and gateways, and between services, is encrypted using TLS (as specified).
    *   **End-to-End Encryption (E2EE):** This can be implemented on the client-side using a library like the Signal Protocol. The server would only see encrypted message blobs, and the `content` field in the database would store this encrypted text. Key management would be handled on the clients.

## 6. System Architecture Diagram (Mermaid Code)

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph "Clients"
        C1[Mobile Client]
        C2[Web Client]
    end

    subgraph "Network & Edge"
        LB[Load Balancer]
        CDN[Media CDN e.g., Cloudflare]
    end

    subgraph "Gateway Layer"
        APIG[API Gateway - HTTP/REST]
        WSG[WebSocket Gateway - Real-time Events]
    end

    subgraph "Backend Microservices"
        MS[Messaging Service]
        PS[Presence Service]
        NS[Notification Service]
        US[User Service]
        MDS[Media Service]
        SS[Search Service]
    end

    subgraph "Data & Messaging Layer"
        DB[(Cassandra DB - Messages, Conversations)]
        Cache[(Redis Cache - Presence, Sessions)]
        Queue[(RabbitMQ / Kafka - Offline Msgs, Notifications)]
        S3[(S3 Object Storage - Media Files)]
        ES[(Elasticsearch - Message Search)]
    end

    subgraph "External Services"
        APNS[Apple Push Notification Service]
        FCM[Google Firebase Cloud Messaging]
    end

    %% Connections
    C1 -- HTTP/S --> LB
    C2 -- HTTP/S --> LB
    LB --> APIG
    LB --> WSG

    APIG -- HTTP --> MS
    APIG -- HTTP --> US
    APIG -- HTTP --> MDS

    WSG -- WebSocket --> C1
    WSG -- WebSocket --> C2
    WSG -- RPC/Events --> MS
    WSG -- RPC --> PS

    MS -- CRUD --> DB
    MS -- Read/Write --> Cache
    MS -- Publishes to --> Queue
    MS -- Calls --> PS
    MS -- Calls --> NS
    MS -- Calls --> SS

    PS -- Read/Write --> Cache

    MDS -- Writes --> S3
    S3 --> CDN
    CDN --> C1
    CDN --> C2

    NS -- Consumes from --> Queue
    NS -- Pushes to --> APNS
    NS -- Pushes to --> FCM

    SS -- Indexes --> DB
    DB -- CDC Stream --> SS
```

Handle 100M+ story views per hour
